subject: system-design
title: Design a Proximity Service (Yelp)
summary: Find the businesses near a location within a radius — a read-heavy lookup whose whole difficulty lives in indexing the surface of the earth so a search reads only nearby cells.

blocks.text: A proximity service answers one question fast: given my location and a radius, which businesses are near me? Yelp, Google Maps, and dating apps all sit on this primitive. The API looks trivial, but the moment you ask "near me" of a table with millions of rows, an ordinary index falls apart — the design lives entirely in how you index space.

items: Search: return businesses within a radius of a latitude/longitude, or inside a map viewport.
Return business details — name, category, rating, address — for results and on a profile page.
Add, update, and delete a business, though this happens rarely.
Non-functional: extremely read-heavy, very low search latency, high availability.

blocks.text: Assume on the order of 200M businesses worldwide and hundreds of millions of searches a day, so a few thousand searches per second at peak. Writes are negligible by comparison — a business's location is set once and almost never changes. The index is built rarely and read constantly, which is exactly the shape that lets you precompute aggressively.

Split the system into two services behind a load balancer. A location-based search service answers "what's near here" against a geospatial index, returning a list of business IDs. A business service holds the full records and serves details. Searches resolve a small set of IDs from the index, then hydrate them from the business store, with both layers cached hard.

items: Search service: maps a (lat, lng, radius) query to nearby business IDs via the geo-index.
Business service: stores and serves the canonical business records, keyed by ID.
Geospatial index: buckets the world into cells so a query touches only nearby buckets.
Cache: hot regions and popular business records served from memory.

blocks.text: A radius search is a 2-D range query, and a normal database index is 1-D — it sorts on one column at a time. The trick is to map two dimensions down to one by bucketing the world into cells, then storing each business under its cell. A search computes the handful of cells covering the radius and reads only those, instead of scanning everything and computing distance to each row.

items: Geohash: interleave latitude and longitude bits into a single string; a shared prefix means physical proximity, so a prefix match returns a cell.
Quadtree: recursively split each region into four until a cell holds few enough businesses, adapting cell size to density.
Google S2: project the sphere onto a cube and number cells along a Hilbert curve, giving uniform cells and clean neighbour math.
All three turn "near me" into "read these few cell buckets," and stitch in neighbouring cells so results near a cell's edge aren't missed.

blocks.title: Why not just a B-tree?
blocks.text: A B-tree on latitude and a B-tree on longitude each answer a 1-D range, but combining them still leaves you scanning a wide band and filtering by true distance. There is no single-column order that keeps points close on the map close in the index. Geohash, quadtrees, and S2 exist precisely to linearise 2-D space so one lookup returns a compact neighbourhood.

The index hands back nearby candidates; ranking decides their order by blending distance with rating, popularity, and relevance to the query. Because businesses move so rarely, the geo-index can be precomputed and replicated read-only across regions, and popular cells cached. The write path — adding or relocating a business — simply recomputes that one record's cell and is cheap at this low write rate.

blocks.title: Takeaway
blocks.text: A proximity service is a read-heavy lookup whose difficulty is entirely spatial. Pick a geospatial index — geohash, quadtree, or S2 — so a radius search reads a few cells instead of the whole table, separate the index from the detail store, and lean on the rare-write nature to precompute and cache.
